## Logistic Regression and GLMs

Today, we begin with a review of a classification method you may
have seen before *logistic regression*. Before getting into the
guts of logistic regression, let's look back at (one of) our 
motivations for (normal) linear regression. 

Linear regression typically assumes the world works something like:

$$ Y = \bx^{\top}\bbeta + \epsilon = \epsilon + \sum_{i=1}^p x_i \beta_i$$

That is, $Y$ is the sum of a 'noise' term $\epsilon$ and a linear signal term
$\bx^{\top}\bbeta$. When we make predictions, we can't predict $Y$ directly
because of the, by definition, unpredictable $\epsilon$ term, so we really
aim for the *conditional mean*, $\E[Y | \bX = \bx] = \bx^{\top}\bbeta$.[^cond]
(Recall that MSE aims for the conditional mean.) This motivates breaking
the model into two distinct parts: 

$$ \begin{align*}
\mu &= \bx^{\top}\bbeta \\
Y &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)
\end{align*}$$



[^cond]: We use a *conditional* mean here because we aren't going for the
'grand average' $Y$, but the $Y$ we expect _with those particular $\bx$ values_.


That is, we combine a linear _mean model_ and then a _noise_ or _sampling_ model
taken from the normal (Gaussian) distribution. We see here that this is a 
(continuous-valued) model not so much because of the mean model, but really
because we used a Gaussian noise distribution. Even if $\bx$ is discrete and
$\bbeta$ are all integers, we could still get any real value out because the
normal distribution can produce any real value (albeit mainly with vanishingly
small probabilities) regardless of the specific mean and standard deviation. 

So how might we extend this set-up to _classification_? Well, the linear
mean model seems fine - just like with regression, it's appealing to start with
linear models - so we really just need to change up the second part, the 
_sampling_ model. For the binary classification context this is quite simple.
We only know one $\{0, 1\}$-distribution, the *Bernoulli*, so let's just sub
that in for the Gaussian.[^bern]

[^bern]: Recall that the *Bernoulli* distribution takes only two values, $1$ and
$0$, with probabilities $p$ and $q = 1-p$. That is $$Z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \implies Z = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{ with probability } 1-p \\ 1 & \text{ with probability } p \end{cases}.$$ 

$$ \begin{align*}
\mu &= \bx^{\top}\bbeta \\
Y &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mu)
\end{align*}$$

This is close, but there are two things that should make us tread gingerly. 
The first is the fact that we've swapped out the 'mean' from the Gaussian with
the 'probability' parameter from the Bernoulli. This is actually a non-issue
because the _mean_ of a Bernoulli is exactly its probability of being $1$: 

$$Z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p) \implies \E[Z] = 0 * (1-p) + 1 * p = p$$

As an aside, this is an _incredibly_ common trick in statistical computing. We
use the 'mean of 0/1 gives a probability' trick all the time with logical 
(TRUE/FALSE) values to estimate probabilities. For instance, in the `penguins`
data set, if we want to estimate the fraction of female penguins in the survey
area: 

```{r}
penguins |>
    mutate(is_female = (sex == "female")) |> # Construct a logical/Boolean value
    summarize(p_female = mean(is_female, na.rm=TRUE))
```

Similarly, if we want to estimate the fraction of `chinstrap` penguins (those 
cute little fellows): 

```{r}
penguins |>
    mutate(is_chinstrap = (species == "Chinstrap")) |> 
    summarize(p_chinstrap = mean(is_chinstrap, na.rm=TRUE))
```

If we're being very formal about this, we might write $\E[1_A] = \P(A)$, but 
we're not going in this direction in this course. (Self-check: why is the mean
always guaranteed to fall in the $[0, 1]$ range and hence be a 
valid probability?)

Ok - so equating means with probabilities for the Bernoulli is harmless. The
other issue is a bit nastier: while the mean can be used as the probability
parameter, we can't use _any_ mean as a probability. In particular, if we
have $\bbeta = -2$ and $\bx = 1$, we get quickly to 
$Y \sim \text{Bernoulli} (-2)$ and a 'probability' of $-2$ is clearly not good
news. So we need one more piece to make this good idea actually work. 

Our problem is that $\bx^{\top}\bbeta$ can take any real value unless we put
*very* strong restrictions on $\bx$ and $\bbeta$, but we only want to put 
$[0, 1]$ values into the Bernoulli. So let's introduce an 'adapter' that will
'squish' $\R$ into the $[0, 1]$ range. Once we do this, we'll certainly have
a workable probability parameter and we should hopefully be good to go. 

Where can we find a function $f: \R \to [0, 1]$? There are many, but the easiest
to work with turns out to be $$f(z) = \frac{e^z}{1 + e^z} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$$
This combines two nice parts: the exponential guarantees us we don't get 
anything negative out and because $1 + e^z > e^z$ for all $z$, we're guaranteed
to be in the $(0, 1)$ range. Graphically, this function looks like: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
data.frame(x = seq(-6, 6, length.out=201)) |> 
    mutate(y = 1/(1 + exp(-x))) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab(expression(z)) + 
    ylab(expression(1 / (1 + e^{-z}))) + 
    ggtitle("Logistic Transform")
```

As you might have guessed, this *logistic* function is the one that gives
*logistic* regression its name. Functions of this shape are generally called
*sigmoidal* (roughly 's-shaped'): they take $-\infty$ to 0, $0$ to $1/2$,
$\infty$ to 1, and monotonically and smoothly map between. 

So this gives us the last piece of our construction: 

$$\begin{align*}
\R \ni \eta &= \bx^{\top}\bbeta = \sum_{i=1}^p x_i \beta_i \tag{Linear Predictor} \\
(0, 1) \ni \mu  &= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}} \tag{Logistic 'Adapter'} \\
Y &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mu) \tag{Bernoulli Sampling Distribution}
\end{align*}$$

Because the last term in this model is still Bernoulli, it's still a $0/1$-type
of model and suitable for binary classification. This is *logistic regression*
we know and love. Returning to the ever-cited penguins, let's build a logistic
regression model to predict `sex` from body measurements and species info, using
$0$ for male and $1$ for female: 

```{r}
penguins |> 
    mutate(is_female = (sex == "female")) |> 
    select(-sex, -island, -year) |> 
    glm(is_female ~ ., data=_, family=binomial) |>
    summary()
```

A few things to note here: 

1) Note that we create our 0/1 (FALSE/TRUE) variable for use in the response
   spot. 
2) Note that we specify the `family` argument as `binomial` here to indicate
   we are doing *logistic* regression. `R` allows us to 'aggregate' 0/1 values
   into a binomial (sum of IID Bernoulli) response - this is sometimes useful
   for things like surveys where you ask many (similar) people the same yes/no
   question. Still, we're really using a "1-count binomial" / Bernoulli here,
   consistent with our derivation.
3) We used an iterative fitting process that took 7 iterations to converge. 
   This is quite fast if you are used to first-order methods, but `R` actually
   uses a _second order_ method (using the first and second derivatives) here
   to solve the problem more rapidly. 
   
Beyond that, this all looks quite similar to regular linear regression. We have
a series of coefficients that tell us the *ceteris paribus* effect of changes.
For instance, as the body measurements gets bigger, we are less likely to have 
a female penguin.[^interp]

[^interp]: This model is to be interpreted _like_ a linear regression model, but
the actual values are quite tricky here because of some of the implicit
correlations between species and body morphology and the more obvious
correlations between pairs of body measurements. Linear-type models are not
quite so easy as we might hope...

So why do we call this model _linear_? Clearly the first part is linear--the
linear predictor--but we 'squish' it through our logistic adapter so we don't
get a 'one-to-one' change in predicted outputs. (In fact, because we have
bounded $[0,1]$ outputs, we can't have a _fully linear_ input/output sort of
response.) Two reasons: 

1) If we represent things on the 'log-odds' scale, so we look not at $\hat{p}$,
   the predicted probability but instead $\log\frac{p}{1-p}$, things are
   actually linear. 
   
   I personally don't find this too compelling because I don't think in terms of
   log odds. 
2) We can compute a 'map' of classifications and see that the boundary is 
   actually linear. 
   
To actually visualize the latter, let's simplify our model to work with only 2
input variables:

```{r}
library(broom)
penguins_logistic_2d <- penguins |> 
    mutate(is_female = (sex == "female")) |> 
    glm(is_female ~ body_mass + flipper_len, data=_, family=binomial) 

penguins_prediction_grid <- expand_grid(
    body_mass = seq(2700, 6300, by=25), 
    flipper_len=seq(172, 231, by=1)
) 

penguins_predictions <- augment(penguins_logistic_2d,
                                newdata=penguins_prediction_grid, 
                                type.predict="response") # Return hat{mu}

ggplot(penguins_predictions, aes(x=body_mass, 
                                 y=flipper_len, 
                                 color=.fitted)) + 
    geom_point() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab("Body Mass") + 
    ylab("Flipper Length") + 
    scale_color_distiller(type="div", palette=3, name="Probability of Female") + 
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

We see here that the 'decision boundary' - the points where we are truly
on the edge and predict $\hat{p}$ - is _linear_. This most fundamentally
is why we call logistic regression a _linear_ model: the 'decision rule'
that comes out of the model is linear. Specifically, we might use something
like

$$\hat{Y} = \text{Female} \text{ if and only if } 0.03 * \text{Body Mass} - \text{Flipper Length} > -75$$

(Numbers are approximate)

```{r}
ggplot(penguins_predictions, aes(x=body_mass, 
                                 y=flipper_len, 
                                 color=.fitted)) + 
    geom_point() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab("Body Mass") + 
    ylab("Flipper Length") + 
    scale_color_distiller(type="div", palette=3, name="Probability of Female") + 
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") + 
    geom_abline(slope=0.03, intercept=75, color="red4")
```

## Classification Boundaries

In our example above, we saw that the boundary line at $\hat{p} = 0.5$ 
was linear. But why did we set the line at $\hat{p} = 0.5$? In this case
(penguin sex guessing), it seems harmless enough, but for more important 
problems, we might want to set our boundaries elsewhere. 


We do so by picking up an idea you might have seen in an economics class: 
utility maximization (or equivalently, loss minimization). We know from our
'2x2 table' that there are 4 possible outcomes: True/False Positive/Negative. 

We can assign a cost or a reward for each outcome and try to determine the
classification rule that maximizes our reward / minimizes our cost. Let's 
suppose I see a Dali etching for sale at a local auction house. The chain of
custody / provenance isn't quite clear, so I don't know if it's a 'true' Dali
or not. I know that if I buy it (let's say for \$500) and get it reviewed by
a proper art authenticator (for another \$1000), I will know if it is a real
Dali or not. If it is a real Dali, I know have a painting I could re-sell 
(now authenticated) for \$5000; if it's not real, I have an attractive print
I could sell for \$50. How confident that the painting is real should I be before
I purchase it? 

Let's work out our four scenarios: 

- True Positive: it is a Dali and I buy it (thinking it is a Dali). I pay
  \$1500 and gain a \$5000 painting, netting me \$3500. 
- False Positive: I buy it (thinking it is a Dali), but it is not authentic.
  I still have to pay \$1500, but now I only have a \$50 print, so I effectively
  lose \$1450. 
- True Negative: I don't think it is a Dali, don't purchase, and spend no
  money on the fake. While I might be proud of myself for loss avoidance, 
  this is a wash.
- False Negative: I don't think it is a Dali, don't purchase it, but it actually
  is! I might feel sad, but financially, this is still a wash. 
  
So let's balance these out: if the probability of being a real Dali (based on
my model) is $\hat{p}$, purchasing has an expected value of: 

$$\E[V_{\text{Buy}}] = \hat{p} * 3500 + (1-\hat{p}) * (-1450) = 5000 \hat{p} -1450$$

Compare this to not purchasing, which always costs me \$0 in this scenario. The
'breakeven' point is: 

$$0 = 5000 * \hat{p} - 1450 \implies \hat{p} = 29\%$$

In this case, I shouldn't actually set my 'buy' decision at 50%, but at the 
more modest level of 29%. (Conveniently, this is still a linear boundary, now
shifted, in logistic regression.)

It is easy to come up with scenarios that produce 'breakeven' points at almost
any $\hat{p}$ by simply playing around with the relevant costs. In general,
as the payoffs become more positive, we are willing to 'bet' more often, while
larger costs make us less likely to 'bet'. 

## Scoring and Calibration

The analysis above relies on a bit of slight of hand: we used it to select 
a decision rule based on our _model probability_, but we computed the rewards
under 'actual probability'. These need not be the same!

Put another way, if our model probabilities are not very accurate, a 30% 
predicted probability doesn't mean a 30% chance in real life and our decision
rule might not be set properly. 

We want our model probabilities to be 'correct' in the following sense: 

- If the model says something should happen 10% of the time for a set of
  predictions, it should happen 10% of the time (in the long run). 
- If the model says something should happen 15% of the time for a set of
  predictions, it should happen 15% of the time (in the long run). 
- If the model says something should happen 20% of the time for a set of
  predictions, it should happen 20% of the time (in the long run). 

and so on for _every_ $p$. A model that has this property is called 
_well-calibrated_ and it is a very nice thing to have!
